name: Brace Up
description: Brandy, absinthe, egg and lemon shaken to a froth. Thomas files it under morning drinks, which tells you what it was for.
funFact: The 1862 book groups a whole shelf of these under recuperatives, and every one of them contains raw egg — the Victorian bar's entire theory of the morning after.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts over.
Strain into a small tumbler.
Grate nutmeg heavily over the top and drink it standing up.

name: Jersey Cocktail
description: Hard cider with sugar and bitters. A cocktail by the 1862 definition, built on cider instead of spirit.
funFact: It qualifies as a cocktail on the original terms — a base, sugar, water and bitters — and proves the definition never actually required a distilled spirit.

steps: Stir the syrup and bitters together in the bottom of a rocks glass.
Add ice.
Pour the cider over slowly so it keeps some of its bubble.
Twist a lemon peel over the top and drop it in.

name: Hot Spiced Rum
description: Rum, butter, sugar and spice under boiling water. The buttered rum before anyone shortened the name.
funFact: The butter is not a garnish or a modern flourish — Thomas prints it in 1862, and it is what keeps the drink from tasting thin.

steps: Put the sugar, butter, cloves and cinnamon in a warmed mug.
Add a splash of boiling water and mash it into a paste.
Pour in the rum and stir.
Top with the rest of the boiling water and grate nutmeg over.
recipe.garnish: Grated nutmeg and a cinnamon stick

name: Champagne Cobbler
description: Champagne over crushed ice with curaçao and fruit. The cobbler template applied to the most expensive bottle in the room.
funFact: The cobbler was the drink that sold the straw — it was among the first served with one, because crushed ice made it impossible to drink any other way.

steps: Fill a goblet with crushed ice.
Add the curaçao and syrup and stir once.
Pour the champagne slowly over the ice so it does not foam over.
Pile fruit and mint on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Seasonal fruit and a mint sprig

name: Port Cobbler
description: Port, sugar and fruit churned through crushed ice. Sweeter and heavier than the sherry version, and older.
funFact: Cobblers were the most-ordered American drink of the 1840s, and the sherry version in particular was what a nineteenth-century bar sold most of.

steps: Muddle the orange slices with the syrup in the bottom of a goblet.
Fill the glass with crushed ice.
Add the port and churn with a barspoon until the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice, pile fruit on top and add a straw.
recipe.garnish: Berries, an orange slice and mint

name: Gin Smash
description: Gin, mint and sugar over crushed ice. A julep in a short glass, which is the only difference there has ever been.
funFact: The old books separate smash from julep purely by glass size — a smash is a short drink and a julep a long one, and nothing else about them differs.

steps: Press the mint gently with the syrup in a rocks glass.
Add the gin and fill with crushed ice.
Churn with a barspoon until the outside of the glass frosts.
Cap with more ice and crown with mint.

name: Santina's Pousse Café
description: Brandy, maraschino and curaçao floated in three clean bands. Named for the New Orleans bartender who worked out how to do it.
funFact: Layering works on sugar content rather than alcohol — the sweeter a liqueur, the denser it is, which is why the syrups always go in first.

steps: Pour the curaçao into a narrow pony glass.
Rest a barspoon just above the surface, curve upward, and pour the maraschino over the back of it.
Float the cognac last, the same way.
Serve without a stirrer — disturbing the layers ruins the drink.
recipe.garnish: None — the three bands are the drink

name: Pousse Café
description: Five or more liqueurs floated in bands, poured heaviest first. Entirely about the pour and not at all about the taste.
funFact: The name means push the coffee — it was served after dinner, alongside coffee, and the more bands a bartender could hold apart the better their reputation.

steps: Pour the grenadine into a tall narrow glass — it is the densest and goes first.
Float each of the others in turn over the back of a barspoon, in the order given.
Pour slowly enough that the stream never breaks the layer beneath.
Serve upright and do not move it quickly.

name: Angel's Kiss
description: Crème de cacao under a float of cream, with a cherry balanced on top. A pousse-café with only two bands.
funFact: It is the simplest drink in the pousse-café family and the one people actually learn on — two liqueurs are hard enough to keep apart.

steps: Pour the crème de cacao into a narrow glass.
Float the cream over the back of a barspoon so it sits in a clean band.
Balance a cherry on the surface of the cream.
Serve without a straw.

name: Widow's Dream
description: Bénédictine shaken with a whole egg and cream. Rich, herbal and almost a dessert.
funFact: Bénédictine's recipe is genuinely secret — the company says three people know it, and holds that only one of them travels at a time.

steps: Dry-shake the Bénédictine and egg without ice for 20 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until cold.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Float the cream over the back of a spoon and grate nutmeg over.

name: Rock and Rye
description: Rye infused with rock candy and fruit. Sold as a cold remedy for most of the nineteenth century, and taxed as one.
funFact: It was marketed as medicine to dodge liquor law, and bottles carried a label claiming it cured colds — which is how a cocktail ended up behind a pharmacy counter.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Barbados Rum Punch
description: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak. The rhyme is the recipe.
funFact: The rhyme is taught to Barbadian children and printed on tea towels, and it scales to any quantity because the ratio is the entire specification.

steps: Combine the lime, syrup, rum and water in a jug and stir.
Add the bitters and stir again — Angostura is not optional here.
Pour over ice in short glasses.
Grate nutmeg heavily over each one.
recipe.garnish: Grated nutmeg and a lime wheel

name: Caudle
description: Hot spiced wine or ale thickened with egg and oatmeal. Half a drink, half a meal, and given to the sick for six hundred years.
funFact: Caudle and posset are sisters — a posset is curdled with wine, a caudle thickened with grain, and both were served to women after childbirth well into the 1800s.

steps: Simmer the oatmeal in the water until it thickens into a thin gruel.
Beat the yolks with the sugar and nutmeg.
Warm the wine and whisk it into the gruel, then temper in the yolks off the heat.
Return to a very low heat and stir until it coats a spoon. Do not let it boil.

name: French 76
description: The French 75 with vodka. Cleaner, colder and with nothing in the way of the champagne.
funFact: The 75 family is numbered by artillery calibre, and the variants that followed kept the joke going by picking bigger guns.

steps: Shake the vodka, lemon juice and syrup with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne so it does not overflow.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.

name: French 125
description: The French 75 rebuilt on cognac, which is what many argue it should have been all along.
funFact: Whether the original took gin or cognac has been argued for a century; the cognac version at least puts a French spirit in a French drink.

steps: Shake the cognac, lemon juice and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with champagne.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Agavoni
description: A Negroni with tequila in place of gin. Same equal thirds, more earth underneath.
funFact: Blanco tequila carries the vegetal edge of cooked agave straight through, which is exactly what Campari's bitterness has something to hold on to.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Tequila Sour
description: Tequila, lemon and sugar with egg white. The sour template on agave, and a Margarita's plainer cousin.
funFact: Lemon rather than lime is what separates this from a Margarita — swap the citrus and the drink stops tasting Mexican and starts tasting like a whiskey sour.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Let the foam settle before garnishing.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cherry

name: Mezcal Sour
description: Mezcal, lime and agave syrup under an egg-white foam that carries the smoke straight up.
funFact: The smoke is not added — mezcal agave is roasted in earth pits lined with hot stones, and the flavour comes from a week underground.

steps: Dry-shake everything without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until very cold.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Dust the foam with chilli salt.
recipe.garnish: A dusting of chilli salt on the foam

name: Toreador
description: Tequila with apricot brandy and lime. One of the first tequila drinks to reach a London bar book.
funFact: Tequila barely appears in English cocktail books before the 1930s, and when it does it is usually spelled wrong and described as a Mexican brandy.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Matador
description: Tequila, pineapple and lime. The easiest agave drink there is, and Trader Vic's answer to the Margarita.
funFact: Pineapple and agave share a green, faintly vegetal note, which is why the pairing works far better than the fruit-juice shortcut it looks like.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Brave Bull
description: Tequila and coffee liqueur over ice. A Black Russian with agave instead of vodka.
funFact: Swap the tequila for vodka and it is a Black Russian; swap it for bourbon and it has no name at all, which is a fair comment on how these drinks get named.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Add the tequila and the coffee liqueur.
Stir briefly to combine and chill.
Twist a strip of lemon peel over the top and drop it in.

name: Chapala
description: Tequila with orange, lime, grenadine and a drop of orange flower water. Named for Mexico's largest lake.
funFact: Orange flower water is measured in drops and turns up in only a handful of classics — this one, the Ramos Gin Fizz, and almost nothing else.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Berta's Special
description: Tequila, honey, lime and soda with an egg white. From a Taxco cantina that has been open since the 1930s.
funFact: Bertita's still stands on the square in Taxco, and the drink is one of very few pre-war Mexican cocktails whose bar of origin is still trading.

steps: Dry-shake the tequila, honey, lime, egg white and bitters without ice.
Add ice and shake hard until cold.
Strain into a tall glass over fresh ice.
Top with soda water and stir once.

name: Picador
description: Tequila, Cointreau and lime, shaken and served up with no salt. The Margarita as a London bar first wrote it down.
funFact: It appears in British books in the 1930s under this name, which puts a Margarita in print in London before the drink had settled on its Spanish one.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Cadillac Margarita
description: A Margarita made with reposado and finished with a float of Grand Marnier poured over the back of a spoon.
glassware: Rocks glass with a salted half-rim
funFact: The float is the whole point — stirred in it disappears, but sitting on top the Grand Marnier hits first and the tequila arrives underneath it.

steps: Salt half the rim of a rocks glass, so the drinker can choose.
Shake the tequila, Cointreau, lime and agave with ice.
Strain into the glass over one large cube.
Float the Grand Marnier over the back of a barspoon.
recipe.garnish: A lime wheel and a salted rim

name: Changuirongo
description: Tequila and whatever soda is cold. Mexico's everyday highball, and deliberately unfussy.
funFact: Grapefruit soda makes it a Paloma and cola makes it a Charro Negro; with anything else it just keeps this name and nobody minds.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the tequila.
Top with whatever cold soda is to hand.
Squeeze a lime wedge in and drop it in the glass.
